notes:
I've written notes on 31 of the 34 verses. Verses 13–15 (the list of Ishmael's sons) are left out because none of the sources I read comment on the individual names. Several requested sources are also missing: I couldn't read NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, Precept Austin, any Orthodox page, or Wesley's notes on wesley.nnu.edu. I found no Anglican, Pentecostal (Assemblies of God), or prosperity/word-of-faith/hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Wesley's and Benson's notes appear only through StudyLight. Luther appears only as quoted by other writers. Most of my searching was used up early, so those gaps reflect limited searching, not proof that these sources say nothing.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Abraham married Keturah after the death of Sarah, recorded in Genesis 23:1-2 and Genesis 23:19. There was nothing wrong with Abraham taking another wife after Sarah's death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/
- Matthew Henry thinks Abraham, now alone, marries Keturah, probably the chief of his maid-servants, born in his house or bought with money. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/25-8.html
- The date is debated. Barnes says that, by the way Hebrew narrative is arranged, this event may have taken place before that recorded in the close of the previous chapter. (same URL) Everett reports scholars who argue that this passage gives no indication that it took place after Sarah's death. He also cites Wenham's view that it is placed at the end of Abraham's story so it doesn't distract from the promise of Isaac. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/genesis-25.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik: These sons would themselves become the fathers of distinct peoples. For example, the Midianites came from Midian. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/genesis/genesis-25.cfm
- He adds that these sons show any fertility problem lay with Sarah, not Abraham. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/
- Matthew Henry sees them as a partial fulfilment of the promise of many descendants. He says this shows how much the virtue of the promise exceeds the power of nature. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_025.cfm

**vv. 3–4**
- The Pulpit Commentary counts six sons, seven grandsons, three great grandsons; in all sixteen descendants. It notes Keil's view that identifying these peoples is uncertain. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-25.html
- Barnes says daughters go unmentioned because it was not customary to mention females, unless they are connected with leading historical characters. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/25-8.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik says Abraham passed on both his wealth and the promise of the land to Isaac. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/
- Matthew Henry puts it this way: since God had already made Isaac heir of the promise, Abraham made him heir of his estate. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/25-8.html

**v. 6**
- Matthew Henry: It was justice to provide for them; parents that do not imitate him in this are worse than infidels. It was prudence to settle them in places distant from Isaac. He also praises Abraham for doing it in his lifetime. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_025.cfm
- Utley (bible.org) gives background from ancient documents. He says the Nuzi Tablets show this was the legally acceptable way to show the father's choice of inheritance and to deal with the semi-legal sons of a concubine. https://bible.org/book/export/html/20848
- Guzik suggests "concubines" may include Keturah, showing she was not on the same level as Sarah in the covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/ Elsewhere he lists Abraham among those with concubines and says the Bible never shows this kind of family life blessed by God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-11/

**v. 7**
- Guzik praises Abraham's long life and says that, though imperfect, he was a man of faith, who had a real relationship with God marked by remarkable obedience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/

**v. 8**
- *"Old and contented":* Clarke sees the picture of a guest regaled by a plentiful banquet. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/25-8.html Constable says the phrase points to an inner peace and satisfaction at death. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/genesis-25.html
- *"Gathered to his people" as a sign of life after death:* this is the broadly shared reading.
  - Keil, quoted in the Pulpit Commentary, says the phrase denotes the reunion in Sheol with friends who have gone before, and therefore presupposes faith in the personal continuance of a man after death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-25.html
  - Gill says it cannot mean his burial, since only Sarah lay in that tomb. It means the admission of his soul into the heavenly state. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/25-8.html
- *A Reformed nuance:* Calvin accepts that the phrase points to a future life. But he will not restrict it, as these expositors do, to the faithful only. In his view all humanity is gathered together in death. (same URL)
- *Matthew Henry's moral point:* death gathers us to those who were "our people" in life, whether God's people or the world's. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_025.cfm
- *Scholarly caution:* the Cambridge Bible says "his people" has no local meaning. It means those of his own family already dead, and now in Sheôl, "the under-world" of departed spirits. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-8.htm Utley adds that Old Testament revelation on the afterlife is shining rather dimly. https://bible.org/book/export/html/20848

**v. 9**
- The Pulpit Commentary says Isaac comes first as heir. It offers three reasons Ishmael joins him: he lived nearer, he had a special blessing, or simply the two eldest sons were honouring their father. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-8.htm
- Barnes calls it brotherly cooperation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/25-8.html
- Matthew Henry notes that no funeral ceremony is recorded. It was the last office of respect they had to pay to their good father. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_025.cfm

**v. 10**
- Constable notes that the cave of Machpelah near Mamre was the old site that later became a part of Hebron. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/genesis-25.html

**v. 11**
- Guzik: Abraham was a great man, but he was only a man. God's work passed on from one generation to the next. Now, God would carry on the work of the covenant first promised to Abraham through Isaac. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/
- Matthew Henry: The blessing of Abraham did not die with him, but survived to all the children of the promise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_025.cfm

**vv. 12–16**
- Matthew Henry says the story turns to Ishmael because God had made promises about him, and we need to see them kept. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_025.cfm
- Guzik reads the "twelve princes" and Ishmael's long life as signs that though he did not receive the Abrahamic covenant, God's blessing and hand was upon him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/

**v. 17**
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that Ishmael's life was nearly 50 years shorter than Isaac's. It asks whether this shows that godliness lengthens life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-25.html

**v. 18**
- Utley sees a fulfilment of Genesis 16:12. He says the phrase is read in many ways, and it is even possible that this refers to military raids against his neighboring relatives. https://bible.org/book/export/html/20848
- Matthew Henry notes the older translation ("he fell in the presence of all his brethren") and two readings of it: "he died" or "his lot fell." Either way, he links it to the word given to Hagar. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_025.cfm

**vv. 19–20**
- Barnes works out that Isaac married in the third year after his mother's death. He says Bethuel is called "the Aramean" because of the country he adopted, not his ancestry. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/25-26.html

**v. 21**
- In the Spanish edition of Enduring Word, Guzik says the promised child doesn't come easily. It comes through prayer and waiting, and a husband's prayers for his wife have special power. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/genesis-25/
- Barnes contrasts Isaac with his father: under a similar trial he did not follow the same crooked policy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-23.htm

**v. 22**
- *How Rebekah "inquired of the LORD":* the Pulpit Commentary reports two views. Some think it was by prayer and sacrifice. Others, including Luther, think she went to a prophet such as Abraham, Melchizedek or Shem. The Pulpit Commentary itself thinks the prophet view unlikely for that period. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-23.htm
- Barnes says the passage hints that there was now a fixed mode and perhaps place of inquiring at the Lord. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/jps/genesis/25-23.html
- Matthew Henry reads the struggle as a picture of the contest between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent (Genesis 3:15). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_025.cfm
- Guzik mentions Jewish legends that the twins tried to kill each other in the womb. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/

**v. 23** (the most debated verse)
- *Traditional reading (nations):* Benson says the twins are the fathers of the Edomites and Israelites. The prophecy was fulfilled in the subjection of the Edomites, for many ages, to the house of David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-23.htm
- *Reformed / Calvinist:*
  - Douglas Moo (on Monergism) says the implications are hotly contested. Calvinists traditionally have found in these verses important support for the notion of unconditional election. He sums up the Arminian alternative: God chooses those he foresees will believe. https://www.monergism.com/israel-and-plan-god-romans-91%E2%80%9329-douglas-moo
  - The Geneva Study Bible's note on v. 32 also uses Reformed language. It says The reprobate do not value God's benefits unless they feel them presently. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-32.htm
- *Methodist / Arminian:* Clarke quotes Dr. Dodd, who says this verse is a key to Romans 9. Dodd argues it proves Romans 9 cannot mean God's arbitrary predestination of particular persons to eternal happiness or misery. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/jps/genesis/25-23.html
- *Guzik (Calvary Chapel; treated here under the Pentecostal/charismatic group):* he takes a middle line. God's choice did not depend on either son's works. But "loved/hated" in Malachi 1 and Romans 9 means more like "accepted/rejected," and God did not hate Esau in the sense of cursing him to a doomed life in either this world or the next. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/
- *Brethren (William Kelly):* the twins had the same parents, so It was therefore impossible to find a closer parity between any than in these two sons of Isaac and Rebecca. Nevertheless, from the first, entirely apart from any grounds such as to determine a preference, God shows that He will be sovereign. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/25-28.html
- *Catholic:*
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia says St. Paul uses this verse to show that in the mystery of election and grace God is bound to no particular nation and is influenced by no prerogative of birth or antecedent merit. https://ccel.org/ccel/herbermann/cathen05.html?term=Esau
  - Augustine reads it morally: it is manifest that under the godly are subdued the ungodly, under the humble are subdued the proud. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801047.htm
- *Modern scholarship (Cambridge Bible):* the verse is in the form of a rhythmic oracle, in four stichoi, or lines. It dates Israel's subjugation of Edom to David's reign (2 Samuel 8:14). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-23.htm

**v. 24**
- Guzik says the visible birth of twins gave reason to believe that what God said about the two boys being fathers of nations and the older serving the younger would also be true. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/

**v. 25**
- Wesley (Methodist) says Esau's name means "made," as if already grown. His hairiness suggested a very robust, daring, active man. But Jacob was smooth and tender as other children. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/25-25.html
- Guzik says "Esau" means "hairy." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/

**v. 26**
- *Meaning of "Jacob":* Clarke derives it from a root meaning to defraud, deceive, to supplant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/25-26.html Guzik says it carried the sense of "trickster," which was not a compliment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/
- *What the heel-grab signified:* Wesley and Benson (both Methodist) follow Matthew Henry. It signified Jacob's pursuit of the birthright and His prevailing for it at last, citing Hosea 12:3. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/25-26.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary notes that Hosea uses the name positively, as a sign of Jacob's favour with God. (same URL)
- *Catholic:* the Catholic Encyclopedia says the name may be short for "Jacob-El" (compare Babylonian *Ya'kub-ilu*). https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/jacob

**vv. 27–28**
- In the Spanish edition of Enduring Word, Guzik says that, as often happens, each parent had a "favourite" son. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/genesis-25/
- Spurgeon: It was a bad thing for the household to be divided as it was—the husband and wife at cross purposes. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons54/sermons54.xxxix.html
- Matthew Henry admires "plain" Jacob: Plain men that have their conversation in simplicity and godly sincerity, and without worldly wisdom, are often found wisest of all for their souls and eternity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_025.cfm

**vv. 29–30**
- On the name Edom, one commentator on the BibleHub page thinks it probably came from Esau's red complexion. His cry for "that red" stew renewed the name. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-31.htm
- The Catholic Encyclopedia infers the sale was widely known from the name itself. The name is rarely used for Esau but almost always for his descendants. https://ccel.org/ccel/herbermann/cathen05.html?term=Esau
- Augustine calls the lentils "Egyptian food." He compares Esau to Israel turning back to Egypt in their hearts (Acts 7:39). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801047.htm

**v. 31**
- *What the birthright was:* Keil says that among the patriarchs it included leadership of the family and the title to the blessing of the promise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-32.htm Matthew Henry says it was Esau's by providence but Jacob's by promise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_025.cfm
- *Was Jacob wrong?*
  - Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary: Jacob was right, that he coveted earnestly the best gifts; he was wrong, that he took advantage of his brother's need. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-32.htm
  - Barnes is gentler. Jacob left Esau free to choose, and His chief error lay in attempting to anticipate the arrangements of Providence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-31.htm
  - Steven Cole (bible.org): as a brother, Jacob should simply have given Esau the soup. He wanted the right thing for the wrong reasons and in the wrong way. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-50-trading-your-soul-what-genesis-2527-34-heb-1216-17
- *Lutheran:* the Spanish Enduring Word page quotes Luther, via Leupold, as saying the deal was not lawful. Jacob was buying what was already his, and Esau was selling what was not his to sell. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/genesis-25/
- *Catholic:* the Catholic Encyclopedia says Jacob, probably knowing the oracle, was quick to draw advantage from the greed of his famished brother. https://ccel.org/ccel/herbermann/cathen05.html?term=Esau
- *Modern critical:* a note on the BibleHub page says Jacob's act is recorded without disapproval. It suggests a touch of humour in the tradition explaining why Israel got richer land than Edom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-31.htm

**v. 32**
- Guzik says Esau wasn't really starving. He meant: "I will die one day anyway, so what good is this birthright to me?" https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/
- Matthew Poole says Esau was thinking of the constant dangers of hunting. This shows his care and affections reached no further than the present life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-32.htm

**v. 33**
- Barnes says Jacob insisted on an oath to have God solemnly called as witness of the transfer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-31.htm
- Keil says the transaction did not justify Jacob's conduct in the matter. Though not condemned here, yet in the further course of the history it is shown to have been wrong. His evidence is that Jacob never used the sale as the basis of a claim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-32.htm

**v. 34**
- *The verb "despised":* Utley says it denotes "to view as worthless" or even "view with contempt." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/genesis-25.html
- *Esau as "profane" (Hebrews 12:16):* the commentators agree on this, and on Esau bearing more blame than Jacob.
  - Keil: Just as Ishmael was excluded from the promised blessing because he was begotten "according to the flesh," so Esau lost it because his disposition was according to the flesh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/25-31.htm
  - Matthew Henry says Esau never tried to undo the sale, which confirmed it after the fact. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_025.cfm
  - Guzik says Esau's character was not the *basis* of God's choice, but it showed the wisdom of that choice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/
- *Baptist (Spurgeon):* Esau's sin consisted in his willingness to sell the Covenant blessing at such a price as that. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons54/sermons54.xxxix.html
- *Application:*
  - Guzik says believers have a birthright in Christ that many trade for passing pleasures. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-25/
  - Cole holds that God is sovereign but people are responsible for their sin. He warns that, like Esau, we can forfeit all these spiritual blessings if we don't appreciate them. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-50-trading-your-soul-what-genesis-2527-34-heb-1216-17
- *Catholic and early Church:*
  - Augustine says Esau loved more that which carnally he desired, than that which spiritually by being born first he had earned. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801047.htm
  - Aphrahat, an early Syriac father (not an Orthodox source I could find), uses Esau as an example of pride brought low. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/370105.htm
  - A Catholic Answers article applies the story to people who leave the Church. It says they have, like Esau, exchanged their birthright for earthly food. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/forfeiting-their-birthright
